claims.text: Migration is a move to live somewhere else; internal migration stays within one country, such as a move from a rural area to a city, and international migration crosses a national border.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Push factors are things about the place of origin that make people want to leave it, and pull factors are things about the destination that attract people to it; a migration usually needs both.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Common push factors are poor harvests, lack of work, low pay and few services in the origin; common pull factors are better-paid jobs, schools and hospitals, family already settled, and safer, more stable conditions in the destination.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Migration streams follow routes people can afford and are allowed to use: distance, cost, borders and information all filter who moves, so most international migrants from a poor region head to the nearest country with work, or to one where relatives have already settled.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Migration has separate impacts on the place left, the place joined and the migrants themselves, and an answer must address the one the question names.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: The origin of a migration stream tends to lose its young adults, so remittances sent home support the families left behind, but the departure of workers of working age can leave too few people to farm the land and care for the old.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: A destination that attracts many migrants tends to gain workers who fill jobs and often do the work local people avoid, but rapid arrivals strain housing and services and can stir resentment, and some migrants struggle in poor-quality housing.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For the migrants themselves, moving can raise pay and open schools and services to their children, but it separates families, and undocumented or unskilled arrivals are open to exploitation and may struggle with the language.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: More than a million people a year move from Mexico to the United States, mostly crossing at the border cities to work in farming, construction and services, in one of the world's largest and longest-running international migration streams.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Mexicans migrate mainly because farm wages in parts of Mexico are far below United States pay: a worker can earn several times more across the border, and family networks in states such as California and Texas settle newcomers into jobs and housing.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: For Mexico, the stream empties villages of working-age adults and brings in the money they send home, which builds houses and keeps children in school; for the United States border states, it supplies labour for agriculture and construction and brings Spanish into daily use.

verification.method: Authored originally for the 0460 learner resource under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires semantic review (RS-28).

claims.text: Remittances, the money migrants send home, reached about 60 billion United States dollars a year to Mexico in the early 2020s, among the largest flows in the world.
